Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

vignette: As a chaplain at a busy hospital, 44-year-old Maya had always been drawn to helping others in their darkest moments. But after surviving a terrorist attack on a crowded train three years ago, she found herself struggling to cope with the aftermath. The traumatic event still felt like yesterday - the smell of smoke and sweat, the sound of screams and shattering glass, the sight of chaos and destruction. When Maya thinks back to that day, it's not just the memories that flood her mind but also a sense of disorientation and confusion. She can't quite put the events in order, and the sensory details feel more vivid than any ordinary memory (Confused Sequence, More Real Than Normal). As she relives those moments, Maya is convinced that she should have done something to prevent it - if only she had been more vigilant or proactive (Bad Coper). Maya's fear of losing control and being at the mercy of events has become an all-consuming concern. She can't bear to be in situations where she feels trapped or helpless, like when people misbehave or authority figures try to exert their power over her (Loss of Control, Avoid Authority Figures). Even positive emotions, like joy or excitement, feel tainted by the memory of that day - as if happiness is a luxury she can no longer afford (Positive Emotion Confusion). In an attempt to regain some sense of control, Maya has developed a range of coping strategies. She performs mental rituals to ward off bad thoughts and prevent another disaster from happening (Magical Prevention). She also restricts her food intake, as if by controlling what goes into her body, she can somehow shield herself from the world's dangers (Undereating). Maya's perceptions of the world have become increasingly distorted. She believes that institutions failed to protect her - if only they had been more vigilant or proactive, the attack might have been prevented (Institutional Failure). As a result, she has lost trust in authority figures and feels like she's on her own in navigating the dangers of life. As Maya navigates her daily environment, she is constantly on high alert. She chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected she feels (Safe Seat Seeking), watches others closely for signs that they might harm her (Watching Others), and is startled by unexpected sounds (Threat in Sounds). Her memories of the event seem to be triggered by these environmental cues, sending her spiraling back into a world of fear and anxiety. Maya's maladaptive strategies have become self-reinforcing. By restricting her food intake or performing mental rituals, she feels like she's taking control - but this only serves to heighten her sense of threat and reinforce her negative appraisals (Maladaptive Strategies → Threat). Her memories of the event continue to haunt her, fueling her fear that the world is a dangerous place (Memory → Negative Appraisals). Despite her best efforts, Maya can't shake off the feeling that she's living on borrowed time. She's started to question whether she's cut out for this line of work - or indeed, whether she's capable of coping with life at all. As she struggles to reconcile her faith with the trauma she's experienced, Maya has come to realize that she needs help - not just to heal from her physical wounds but also to repair the emotional and psychological damage that still lingers. It was this growing awareness of her own limitations and vulnerabilities that finally brought Maya to seek professional help. She hopes that therapy will allow her to process her memories and emotions in a healthier way, and perhaps even learn to trust herself - and others - once again. But for now, the fear and anxiety remain, a constant reminder of the trauma she's endured and the long road ahead.
